questions.stem: How many electrons do Group 7 elements have in their outer shell?
questions.explanation: All Group 7 elements (halogens) have 7 electrons in their outer shell. They need to gain just 1 electron to achieve a stable full outer shell.

questions.stem: What happens to the reactivity of halogens as you go down Group 7?
questions.explanation: Reactivity decreases down Group 7 because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder to attract and gain an extra electron. Fluorine is the most reactive halogen.

questions.stem: What happens when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution?

options.text: The solution turns orange-brown as chlorine displaces bromine

questions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from potassium bromide. The solution turns orange-brown due to the presence of bromine: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.

questions.stem: What type of ion do halogens form when they react with metals?
questions.explanation: Halogens gain 1 electron to form 1- ions (halide ions), such as Cl⁻, Br⁻, and I⁻. This gives them a stable full outer shell.

questions.stem: What is the state of bromine at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Bromine is a red-brown liquid at room temperature. It is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature. It produces an orange-brown vapour.

questions.stem: In a halogen displacement reaction, a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one. Which of the following reactions would NOT occur?

options.text: Chlorine displacing bromine from sodium bromide
Fluorine displacing chlorine from sodium chloride
Iodine displacing chlorine from sodium chloride
Bromine displacing iodine from potassium iodide

questions.explanation: Iodine cannot displace chlorine because iodine is less reactive than chlorine. A halogen can only displace a less reactive halogen below it in the group.

questions.stem: What trend is observed in the melting and boiling points of halogens going down Group 7?
questions.explanation: Melting and boiling points increase down Group 7 because the molecules become larger with more electrons, leading to stronger intermolecular forces (London dispersion forces).
